title: Research Data Series: Index of Common Inflation Expectations
summary: The Federal Reserve Board publishes the Index of Common Inflation Expectations (CIE), a dynamic factor model that summarizes comovement across various inflation expectations measures. The original March 2021 note announces this quarterly research data series, with updates posted at noon Eastern Time on the third Friday of January, April, July, and October. The April 2022 update introduced methodological changes including new survey data from the NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations and modifications to the autoregressive process order.
key_points: CIE summarizes inflation expectations using a dynamic factor model, projected onto SPF 10-year PCE inflation and Michigan 5-10 year measures
April 2022 update added NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations 1-year and 3-year measures and Michigan Survey 25th/75th percentile measures
April 2022 update removed 5-year TIPS breakeven inflation as redundant and redefined Livingston Survey measure to G_ZM_To_12M
Updated index assumes autoregressive process of order 5 for the latent factor dynamics
Original CIE columns phased out by October 2022; current columns are CIE_spf and CIE_mich
The CIE is explicitly labeled as experimental research, published for informational purposes only, and may be discontinued at any time
why_it_matters: This research data series provides a consolidated signal of inflation expectations drawn from multiple surveys and market-based measures (SPF, Michigan, NY Fed SCE, Livingston Survey, TIPS breakevens). As a macro indicator, the CIE aggregates common movements in inflation expectations. The source itself describes the index construction methodology and update schedule rather than providing current readings or interpretations of current market conditions. The CIE is explicitly experimental and disclaimer-labeled for informational use only.
macro_context: The CIE tracks common movements in inflation expectations across multiple data sources including surveys (SPF, Michigan, Livingston, NY Fed SCE) and market-based measures (TIPS breakevens). As a macro indicator, it could signal changes in inflation anchoring if it diverges from the Fed's 2% target, but the source itself does not provide current readings or interpret market conditions.
